tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: TradingAgents is a multi-agent LLM trading framework that mirrors a real trading firm: analysts gather evidence, bull and bear researchers debate it, a trader drafts a proposal, a risk team challenges it, and a portfolio manager makes the final call. The README covers that architecture plus installation, Docker, required APIs, CLI and Python package usage, checkpoint recovery and evaluation. Keep this cast of roles in mind, because each later step maps one of them to code.

tour.title: Packaging and First Run
tour.description: pyproject.toml declares the distribution: its LangChain, LangGraph, yfinance, rich and typer dependencies, optional extras, and the `tradingagents` console script. main.py is the smallest way to use the library: it builds the default config, creates a TradingAgentsGraph in debug mode and propagates a single NVDA decision. Every other entry point, including the CLI you'll meet later, is a richer version of these few lines.
tour.languageLesson: pyproject.toml is the modern, single place to declare Python packaging. `[project.scripts]` turns a Python function into a shell command when the package is installed, and optional dependency groups (extras) let users run `pip install tradingagents[bedrock]` only when they need them.

tour.title: Configuration and Secrets
tour.description: default_config.py is the most depended-on module in the project. It defines the built-in defaults for LLM providers, data vendors, paths and limits, and folds in TRADINGAGENTS_* environment overrides with type-driven coercion. The package root loads .env files at import so every entry point sees API keys, and .env.example lists the keys for each supported provider. dataflows/config.py binds a per-run copy of this config to a ContextVar, so two graphs running at once each read their own vendor settings.
tour.languageLesson: Python's `contextvars.ContextVar` holds a value that is local to the current execution context (thread or asyncio task). It works like a global setting that can't leak between concurrent runs, which is why it suits per-run configuration.

tour.title: Pluggable LLM Clients
tour.description: The framework is provider-agnostic. factory.py lazily creates the right client for each model tier from the config, so the analysts and the managers can run on different providers. base_client.py defines the abstract interface and normalizes each provider's message content into plain text. openai_client.py covers the whole OpenAI-compatible family through a declarative registry, and capabilities.py records which parameters and structured-output methods each model supports.
tour.languageLesson: This is the Factory pattern combined with an abstract base class (`abc.ABC`). Callers depend only on the BaseLLMClient interface, and the factory decides which concrete subclass to build, so adding a provider doesn't touch any agent code.

tour.title: Shared State and Ratings
tour.description: Before looking at the graph, learn the data it passes around. state.py defines the TypedDict schemas for the overall LangGraph agent state and for the investment and risk debate sub-states. schemas.py defines the Pydantic models for structured outputs (ResearchPlan, TraderProposal, PortfolioDecision, SentimentReport). rating.py fixes the shared five-tier rating scale and returns REVIEW instead of silently defaulting to Hold when no rating can be read.
tour.languageLesson: `TypedDict` gives a plain dict static type hints, which LangGraph uses to describe the state channels. Pydantic `BaseModel` validates and coerces data at runtime, which suits parsing LLM output that may be malformed.

tour.title: The TradingAgentsGraph Orchestrator
tour.description: trading_graph.py is the hub of the system and imports more modules than any other file. It creates the tier LLM clients from Step 4, compiles the graph, runs or streams propagation with checkpointing, settles past decisions in the memory log, and records decisions and reports. propagation.py builds the initial state from Step 5 for a ticker and date and supplies the invocation arguments, such as the stream mode and recursion limit.

tour.title: Wiring the LangGraph Workflow
tour.description: setup.py builds and compiles the LangGraph StateGraph. It wires a tool-loop subgraph for each analyst, the researcher debate, the trader, the risk debate and the portfolio manager together with conditional edges. conditional_logic.py decides when each debate continues or hands off, based on round limits, and analyst_execution.py turns the user's analyst picks into an ordered execution plan. checkpointer.py stores SQLite checkpoints per ticker with deterministic thread IDs, so an interrupted run can resume.
tour.languageLesson: In LangGraph, a StateGraph is built from nodes (functions that read state and return updates) and edges. `add_conditional_edges` takes a routing function that returns the name of the next node, which is how loops such as a multi-round debate are expressed.

tour.title: The Analyst Team
tour.description: Analysts are the first stage of the pipeline. Each file is a factory that returns a LangGraph node: the Market Analyst reads prices, indicators and a verified snapshot; the News Analyst covers company, global, macro and prediction-market news; the Fundamentals Analyst reads statements and insider trades; and the Sentiment Analyst reads Yahoo headlines, StockTwits and Reddit. turn.py runs one tool-using turn and, once the tool rounds are used up, a final turn without tools so every analyst always finishes its report.
tour.languageLesson: Each `create_*` function is a closure: it captures the LLM and configuration when it's called and returns an inner function that LangGraph calls later with only the state. This keeps node signatures uniform while letting each node carry its own dependencies.

tour.title: Tools and the Data Router
tour.description: tools.py exposes the LangChain tools the analysts from Step 8 call. Each tool injects the run's trade date, so a model can't ask for data from the future. router.py maps each tool category and method to vendor implementations (yfinance, Alpha Vantage, SEC EDGAR, FRED, Polymarket) with configurable fallback chains. errors.py defines the vendor error types, which let the router react to how a failure behaves rather than to which vendor raised it.

tour.title: Point-in-Time Data Vendors
tour.description: Preventing look-ahead bias is the main design goal of the data layer. date_window.py holds the shared rules: it clamps requested dates to the trade date, filters items to the right window, reports coverage gaps, and withholds live-only data from historical runs. The Yahoo OHLCV loader caches prices and guards against stale data, snapshot.py builds a fixed set of verified market numbers so models don't make up figures, and sec_edgar.py serves financial figures only as they were filed on or before the run date.

tour.title: Research Debate and Trader
tour.description: With the analyst reports written, the Bull and Bear Researchers argue opposite cases over several rounds, using the routing logic from Step 7. The Research Manager judges the debate and produces a structured ResearchPlan with a five-tier rating. The Trader then turns that plan and the market report into a TraderProposal with price levels. structured.py binds each model to its schema from Step 5 and falls back to free text if structured output fails.

tour.title: Risk Debate and Final Decision
tour.description: The trader's proposal is challenged by three risk debaters: an Aggressive one favoring high reward, a Conservative one protecting capital, and a Neutral one weighing both. The Portfolio Manager reads that debate, the caller's portfolio context and lessons from past decisions, and produces the final structured PortfolioDecision. portfolio.py models the caller's positions and renders them for these decision agents.

tour.title: Memory, Reflection and Backtesting
tour.description: Decisions don't end when the graph does. log.py stores each decision and its rating in a Markdown-backed memory log. Once a holding window has traded, settlement.py fetches final closes and computes raw and benchmark-relative returns. reflection.py asks an LLM to write a lesson from each settled outcome, and the Portfolio Manager from Step 12 reads those lessons on later runs. backtest.py runs the graph over a grid of tickers and dates against an isolated log and summarizes hit rates and alpha.

tour.title: The Interactive CLI
tour.description: cli/main.py is the Typer application behind the `tradingagents` command, with analyze (the default), backtest, login and logout commands. selections.py collects every run choice, either interactively or from flags and environment variables, and checks providers and API keys. run.py builds the run config, streams the TradingAgentsGraph from Step 6 into the live Rich display in display.py, and offers to save the reports that reporting.py writes as Markdown.
tour.languageLesson: Typer builds a command-line interface from ordinary Python functions: type hints on the parameters become typed options and arguments. Rich's `Live` context re-renders a layout in place, which is how the CLI shows agent status updating in real time.

tour.title: Containers, CI and Releases
tour.description: The Dockerfile uses a multi-stage Python 3.13-slim build that installs the package into a virtualenv, then copies it into a runtime image that runs as a non-root user with the CLI as its entrypoint. docker-compose.yml runs that CLI interactively and adds an optional Ollama profile for local models, with named volumes to keep data. CI runs pytest on Python 3.11 to 3.14 plus a non-UTC timezone run, a clean-install smoke test and strict ruff linting. The release workflow checks the version against the tag and publishes a tested wheel.
tour.languageLesson: Multi-stage Docker builds use several FROM statements. The builder stage keeps compilers and build tools, and the runtime stage copies only the finished virtualenv, so the final image is smaller and exposes less. Compose profiles let optional services such as Ollama start only when you ask for them.
